## 🏠 Minimum Barrier Height – Deck on a House

Under **NZ Building Code Clause F4 – Safety from Falling**, Acceptable Solution **F4/AS1 Table 1**:

| Location | Minimum Height |
|---|---|
| **Balconies and decks** (detached dwellings & household units) | **1000 mm** |
| Stairs and ramps within a dwelling | 900 mm |

> Height is measured **vertically from finished floor level** (ignoring thin coverings like carpet or vinyl).

---

### 🔑 Key additional requirements for housing:
- **Opening sizes** must be small enough that a **100 mm diameter sphere cannot pass through** anywhere in the barrier (to protect children under 6).
- On stairs, the triangular gap formed by the riser, tread, and bottom rail must not allow a **150 mm diameter sphere** through.
- Horizontal rails that run the full height of a barrier are **not recommended** as they can be easily climbed by young children — vertical members are preferred.

---

> ⚠️ **This is general Building Code guidance, not project-specific advice.** Please confirm all requirements against the current official MBIE document and with your designer or building consent authority, especially for anything safety-critical.

## 🏊 Residential Swimming Pool Fence (Barrier) Height — NZ Building Code

### Minimum Height: **1200 mm (1.2 metres)**
Under **F9/AS1 clause 2.1.2**, pool barriers that are **not on a property boundary** must be **at least 1200 mm high**, measured from the finished ground or floor level on the **outside** of the barrier.

---

### Key Additional Requirements:
- **No climbable gaps:** No openings in the barrier that a **100 mm diameter sphere** could pass through.
- **Angle:** Barriers must not lean more than **15° from vertical**, and may only slope *away* from the pool.
- **Horizontal rails:** If rails/wires are not vertical, they must be at least **900 mm apart** vertically to restrict climbing.
- **Climbing hazards:** No ground features or objects **within 1200 mm of the top** of the barrier on the outside that could help a child climb over.
- **Wire mesh panels:** If the mesh openings are between **13 mm and 35 mm**, the barrier must be at least **1800 mm high**.

### Consent Required:
Pool barriers always require a **building consent** — they are specifically excluded from the consent-not-required exemption for general fences.

---

> ⚠️ **This is general Building Code guidance, not project-specific advice.** Always confirm requirements against the [current official MBIE documents](https://www.building.govt.nz) and consult your designer or consent authority for anything safety-critical.

## 🚿 Maximum Hot Water Temperature at Baths & Showers in a House

Under **Clause 6.14.1 (Maximum temperatures)** of G12/AS1, the delivered hot water temperature at the outlet of any sanitary fixture used for personal hygiene **must not exceed:**

| Building Type | Maximum Temperature |
|---|---|
| **Houses and all other buildings** (residential) | **50°C** |
| Early childhood centres, schools, old people's homes, hospitals, and institutions for people with psychiatric or physical disabilities | **45°C** |

> ⚠️ **Note:** The Ministry of Education also requires water from taps accessible to children in early childhood centres not to exceed **40°C** for licensing purposes.

---

### 🔑 Key Points for a Residential House:
- The **maximum is 50°C** at the outlet (bath, shower, basin, bidet).
- A **tempering valve (TV) or thermostatic mixing valve (TMV)** must be installed to limit delivery temperature — compliant devices are listed in Table 8B of G12/AS1.
- The **storage water heater thermostat must still be set to at least 60°C** (Clause 6.14.3) to prevent the growth of **Legionella bacteria** — the tempering/mixing valve then brings the delivered temperature down to a safe level.

---

*This is general Building Code guidance, not project-specific advice. Always confirm against the current official MBIE document and check with your plumber or designer for anything safety-critical.*

## Minimum Cladding Clearance Above a Paved Surface

Under **E2/AS1, Paragraph 9.1.2.6**, the base of a wall cladding system must finish a minimum of:

| Surface Type | Minimum Clearance |
|---|---|
| **Paved surface** | **100 mm** |
| **Unpaved (bare ground)** | **175 mm** |
| **Roof cladding or membrane deck** | **35 mm** |

> *"the base of the cladding system shall finish a minimum of 100 mm above a paved surface"* — E2/AS1, Paragraph 9.1.2.6(a)(i)

---

### A few important details to keep in mind:

- The cladding must also **overlap the concrete slab by 50 mm** (9.1.2.6(b)).
- For **direct-fixed claddings**, there must be a minimum **6 mm horizontal offset** to prevent capillary action (9.1.2.6(c)).
- For **masonry veneer**, different clearances apply — refer to Table 9.1.2.1.
- **Reduced clearances** (e.g., above well-drained paving sheltered under a roof overhang) may sometimes be acceptable but must be designed and assessed as an **alternative solution**.
- The clearance is measured to the **finished plane of the adjacent horizontal surface** (9.1.2.3).
- These clearances must also be **maintained ongoing** as part of regular building maintenance (2.2.2.1(c)).

---

## Private Stairway Dimensions (NZ Building Code D1/AS1 — Table 6)

There are three categories of private stairway, each with different limits:

| Stair Type | Max Pitch | **Max Riser Height** | **Min Tread (Going)** |

| **Minor private** (infrequent access to a single non-living room) | 47° | **220 mm** | **220 mm** |

- **Uniformity** — riser heights and tread depths within a single flight must be **uniform within ±5 mm**.

- **Landings** — the maximum rise between landings for a private stairway is **4.0 m**.
- **Handrails** — required on at least one side for stairways with two or more risers (may be omitted for two or three risers within or giving access to a household unit).

## Maximum Gradient for an Accessible Ramp — NZ Building Code

Under **Acceptable Solution D1/AS1 (Table 3)**, the maximum slopes for ramps are:

| Type of Ramp | Maximum Slope |
|---|---|
| **Accessible ramp** | **1:12** |
| Common ramp (subject to wetting) | 1:10 |
| Common ramp (normally dry) | 1:8 |
| Service ramps | 1:3 |

So **1 in 12** is the steepest gradient permitted for an accessible ramp.

---

### Other key requirements for accessible ramps to keep in mind:
- **Maximum rise between landings:** 750 mm (the reasonable maximum for a wheelchair user to negotiate)
- **Landing length:** minimum 1200 mm
- **Minimum clear width:** 1200 mm
- **Edge protection:** A minimum **75 mm upstand** is required on any drop-off side
- **Handrails:** Required on both sides where the ramp slope is steeper than **1 in 20**, with a 300 mm horizontal extension at each end
- **Cross fall:** No steeper than **1:50**

---

> ⚠️ **This is general Building Code guidance only — not project-specific advice.** Always confirm requirements against the current official MBIE document and with your designer or engineer for anything safety-critical.

## 🏗️ Durability Requirements for Structural Framing

### **50 Years — the standard requirement**

Structural framing must last a minimum of **50 years**. This applies because:

- Any building element that **provides structural stability** to the building requires **≥ 50 years** durability (Step 2 of the assessment framework in B2/AS1).
- Structural framing is also typically **difficult to access or replace** (requiring significant removal of other elements), which independently triggers the 50-year requirement.

### Specific framing elements confirmed at 50 years in Table C.1.1.1:

| Element | Situation | Requirement |
|---|---|---|
| **Wall framing** (timber or steel), including dwangs/nogging | **Load-bearing framing** | ≥ 50 years |
| **Wall framing** (timber or steel) | Easy-to-access lined, non-load-bearing partitions | ≥ 15 years |
| **Wall framing** (timber or steel) | Easy-to-access unlined, non-structural/demountable partitions | ≥ 5 years |
| **Structural steel** | All situations | ≥ 50 years |
| **Bracing elements** (all fixings included) | All situations | ≥ 50 years |
| **Sub-floor structure** | All situations | ≥ 50 years |

---

### Key takeaway for your site team:
> **Load-bearing/structural framing = 50 years minimum, no exceptions.** Non-structural or easily demountable framing may have a reduced requirement (15 or 5 years), but anything carrying loads needs to be specified and treated accordingly.

---

*This is general Building Code guidance, not project-specific advice. Always confirm requirements against the current official MBIE documents and your project designer — especially for anything safety-critical.*

## 🪟 Natural Ventilation – Openable Window Area for a Bedroom

### Standard Rule (most houses)
> **Net openable area ≥ 5% of the bedroom's floor area**

So for example:
| Bedroom floor area | Min. openable window area |
|---|---|
| 10 m² | 0.5 m² |
| 12 m² | 0.6 m² |
| 15 m² | 0.75 m² |

- The **net openable area** is measured on the **face dimensions** of the window (i.e., the actual opening, not the full frame).
- Openable windows/doors used for ventilation must be able to be **fixed in the open position** during normal occupancy.

---

### Special Case – Only One External Wall (e.g. apartments)
If the bedroom has only one external wall, the same **5% of floor area** rule applies, but there are additional requirements:
- The distance from the external wall to the opposing wall must be **less than 6 metres**.
- **Trickle ventilators** must also be installed (sized based on number of occupants per Tables 2.2.2.5A & 2.2.2.5B in G4/AS1).

### If the Bedroom Has No Direct Outside Opening
It can be ventilated via an adjacent habitable space (not a bathroom, kitchen, toilet, or laundry), but openings and trickle ventilators must be sized to the **combined floor area** of both spaces.

---

> ⚠️ **This is general Building Code guidance, not project-specific advice.** Always confirm requirements against the current official MBIE documents and with your designer or consent authority — especially for anything safety-critical.

## 🔊 NZ Building Code – Sound Insulation Between Apartments (Clause G6)

Sound insulation between apartments (referred to in the Code as **abutting occupancies / household units**) is governed by **NZBC Clause G6 – Airborne and Impact Sound**.

### Minimum Performance Requirements

| Element | Rating Required |
|---|---|
| **Walls, floors & ceilings** (airborne sound) | **STC ≥ 55** (Sound Transmission Class) |
| **Floors** (impact sound) | **IIC ≥ 55** (Impact Insulation Class) |

These apply to **all building elements common between occupancies** — e.g., party walls, separating floors, and ceilings between apartments.

---

### Key Points

- **STC 55** is the minimum for all separating walls, floors, and ceilings between units.
- **IIC 55** is the minimum for separating floors to control impact noise (footsteps, etc.).
- The Acceptable Solution **G6/AS1** provides prescriptive construction details (specific wall, floor, and ceiling assemblies) that are deemed to comply. These typically involve:
  - **Physical separation** (e.g., staggered stud or double leaf walls)
  - **Acoustic insulation** (min. 10 kg/m³ glass fibre)
  - **Carpet on underlay** (where shown in the figures — this is a requirement, not optional)
  - **Airtight sealing** of all joints and penetrations
- The **Verification Method G6/VM1** allows testing to ASTM E413 as an alternative compliance pathway.

---

> ⚠️ **This is general Building Code guidance, not project-specific advice.** Always confirm requirements against the current official MBIE documents and with your acoustic designer/engineer, especially for anything safety-critical or where alternative solutions are proposed.

## 🔔 Smoke Alarms in a House (NZ Building Code)

### What type is required?
For a standard house (referred to as **Risk Group SH** – Single Household), the acceptable solution requires a **Type 1 – Domestic Smoke Alarm System**. This is:
- One or more **interconnected smoke alarm devices**, each with a smoke detector and audible alarm
- Must comply with **NZS 4514:2021** (Interconnected smoke alarms for houses)
- No connection to a remote receiving centre is required

> *"The minimum fire safety system required in household units is now specified as interconnected smoke alarms complying with NZS 4514:2021"* — C/AS1 (second edition, amendment 1)

---

### Where do they go?
The Building Code Acceptable Solution (C/AS1) requires smoke alarms in **every household unit**, but the specific **room-by-room placement rules** (e.g., in every bedroom, in hallways, on every level) are set out in **NZS 4514:2021** itself — the standard to which C/AS1 directly refers. The key principles from NZS 4514 (as widely applied in NZ practice) are:

| Location | Requirement |
|---|---|
| **Every bedroom / sleeping area** | ✅ Required |
| **Hallway outside bedrooms** | ✅ Required |
| **Every level of the house** | ✅ At least one per floor |
| **Living/lounge areas** | ✅ Generally required |
| **Kitchen** | ⚠️ Avoid direct placement over the stove (use heat alarm or locate away from cooking appliances to reduce nuisance alarms) |
| **Garage / bathrooms** | ❌ Generally not required |

All alarms must be **interconnected** — if one goes off, they all go off.

---

### Key points for the site team:
- Alarms must be **manufactured and installed** in accordance with **NZS 4514**
- Interconnection is now the minimum standard — wireless interconnection is acceptable under NZS 4514:2021
- Placement details (ceiling vs wall, distances from corners/vents, etc.) are specified within NZS 4514 — your installer/electrician should follow this standard directly

---

> ⚠️ **This is general Building Code guidance only — not project-specific.** Always confirm exact alarm locations against your consented plans, your designer's specifications, and the current NZS 4514:2021 standard. For anything safety-critical, check with your designer or building consent authority.

---

## 🌧️ Design Storm Events for Surface Water Drainage (House)

The Building Code sets **two separate storm event thresholds**, each with a different purpose:

### 1. **10% Annual Exceedance Probability (AEP) — 1-in-10-year event**
> *E1.3.1* — Surface water collected or concentrated by buildings or sitework **shall be disposed of** in a way that avoids damage or nuisance to **other property**.

This is your **drainage design event** — gutters, downpipes, and site drainage must be sized to handle this event without causing problems for neighbours or adjacent property.

---

### 2. **2% Annual Exceedance Probability (AEP) — 1-in-50-year event**
> *E1.3.2* — Surface water **shall not enter the building** (this applies specifically to Housing, Communal Residential, and Communal Non-residential buildings).

This drives your **minimum floor level** — the house floor must be set high enough that a 1-in-50-year event cannot get inside.

---

### 📐 In Practice
- **Gutters, downpipes, and site drains** → design to the **10% AEP (1-in-10 year)** event
- **Floor level** → set to be above the **2% AEP (1-in-50 year)** flood level
- Rainfall intensity data can come from your **Territorial Authority, NIWA HIRDS**, or the tables in E1/AS2 — use the most conservative source

> ⚠️ **Important:** Your local Territorial Authority or district plan may impose stricter floor level or drainage requirements than the Building Code minimums (e.g., some councils use 1% AEP / 1-in-100-year for floor levels in flood-prone areas). Always confirm with your designer and the current official MBIE documents for anything safety-critical.

## 🏠 Roof Insulation R-Value — New House in Auckland

### Auckland's Climate Zone
Auckland falls in **Climate Zone 1** (the warmest zone) under the NZ Building Code.

---

### Minimum Roof/Ceiling R-Value (H1/AS1 — Calculation Method)

Under **H1/AS1 (Sixth Edition, effective 27 November 2025)**, the minimum construction R-value for a roof/ceiling is:

| Building Element | Minimum Construction R-Value |
|---|---|
| **Roof / Ceiling** | **R2.6 (m²·K/W)** |
| Walls | R1.0 |
| Floors (non-slab) | R1.3 |

> ⚠️ This **R2.6 is a construction R-value** (not just the insulation batt R-value). It accounts for the whole roof/ceiling assembly including framing. The insulation batt itself will typically need to be rated higher (e.g. R3.2 or R3.6 batts) to achieve a construction R-value of R2.6 once thermal bridging through framing is factored in. Check the **BRANZ House Insulation Guide (6th edition)** for typical assembly combinations.

---

### Key Points to Note

1. **Minimum floor for the whole roof area** — even along the ceiling perimeter (e.g. where rafters compress insulation), the R2.6 construction R-value must still be maintained throughout.
2. **Heated ceilings** (e.g. in-ceiling radiant systems) have a much higher minimum of **R6.6** — same for all climate zones.
3. The **modelling pathway (H1/VM1)** is an alternative if you want design flexibility, but the reference building R-value used for roofs is R6.6 across all zones, so exceeding the minimum will generally be beneficial.
4. Insulation must be installed per **NZS 4246** to achieve the intended performance.

---

Source: *H1 Energy Efficiency AS1 (sixth edition) · page 11 of 55* and *page 8 of 55*

## 🚽 Toilets Required for a Household Unit (Dwelling)

Under **Acceptable Solution G1/AS1** (Personal Hygiene), **Table 1** sets out the minimum number of sanitary fixtures required by building type.

For **detached dwellings and multi-unit dwellings**, the requirement is straightforward:

| Building Use | User Group | WC Pans (Unisex) | Basins (Unisex) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Detached dwellings & multi-unit dwellings | Occupants | **1** | **1** |

So, the Building Code requires a **minimum of 1 toilet (WC pan) and 1 basin** for a household unit, regardless of the number of occupants.

> 📌 **Note:** G1/AS1 also requires that WC pans and basins must be provided in any building where people **live or are accommodated** (G1/AS1 paragraph 1.1.2).

answer:
Great question! Here's a summary of the **maximum open path travel distances for escape** under the NZ Building Code Acceptable Solutions. Note that the limits depend on **which Acceptable Solution applies**, the **building/risk group**, and **what fire systems are installed**.

---

## C/AS1 — Household Units & Outbuildings (Table 3.3.1.1)

| Portion of Escape Route | No System | Type 1 System | Type 1 System + Sprinklers |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Dead End Open Path (DEOP)** | 20 m | 35 m | 40 m |
| **Total Open Path (TOP)** | 50 m | 75 m | 100 m |

---

## C/AS2 — All Other Buildings (Table 3.3.1.1)

Distances vary by **risk group** and **fire system type**. Key examples:

| Risk Group | Portion | No System / Type 2 | Type 4 / Type 5 | Type 6 | Type 7 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **SM** (Sleeping – managed) | DEOP / TOP | 20 m / 50 m | 30 m / 75 m | 30 m / 75 m | 40 m / 100 m |
| **CA** (Commercial) | DEOP / TOP | 20 m / 50 m | 40 m / 100 m | 40 m / 100 m | 50 m / 120 m |
| **WB** (Workplace – low hazard) | DEOP / TOP | 25 m / 60 m | 50 m / 120 m | 50 m / 120 m | 75 m / 150 m |
| **VP** (Vulnerable persons) | DEOP / TOP | 35 m / 90 m | — | 70 m / 180 m | — |

> If the total open path travel distance to a final exit exceeds the allowable limit, the remainder of the escape route must be a **safe path**.

---

## Key Measurement Rules (both AS1 & AS2)
- **Start point:** Measured from no more than **1.0 m** from the most remote point in the space.
- **Obstructions:** If furniture/fittings locations are unknown, measure **orthogonally** (right-angle grid method).
- **Stairs:** Open path taken as the **plan length** on the stair centreline plus landings.
- **Ladders:** Open path taken as the **vertical height**.

---

> ⚠️ **This is general Building Code guidance, not project-specific advice.** Always confirm distances against the current official MBIE documents and with your fire engineer or designer — especially for safety-critical decisions.
